lead: FIRST(α) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α. FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately after nonterminal A in some sentential form. A predictive parser uses these sets to pick one production without guessing, and to recover from errors. Only a few universities teach FIRST and FOLLOW as a separate exam topic; most fold it into LL(1) table construction. You meet them again in 2.6.
prereq: You need: 2.2 for derivations, 2.3 for grammar form, and the idea of a nullable symbol.

blocks.text: ε is the empty string. A nonterminal A is nullable if A ⇒* ε. In the grammar below, E′ and T′ are nullable.

items: If X → ε, add ε to FIRST(X).
If X → Y₁Y₂…Yₖ, add FIRST(Y₁) − {ε}. If Y₁ is nullable, add FIRST(Y₂) − {ε}, and continue while symbols are nullable. If all symbols are nullable, add ε.

blocks.text: For a string α, scan left to right. Stop at the first non-nullable symbol. ε is in FIRST(α) only if every symbol is nullable. Example: FIRST(T E′) = FIRST(T) = {(, id}; T is not nullable. FIRST(E′) = {+, ε}. FIRST(+ T E′) = {+}. FIRST(ε) = {ε}.
ε is a flag that the string can vanish. It is not a terminal. Never put ε into FOLLOW.
FOLLOW(A) is defined only for a nonterminal A. It holds terminals that can appear right after A in a sentential form, plus $, the end marker. If A can be last, $ is in FOLLOW(A).

items: Put $ in FOLLOW(S) for start symbol S.
For A → α B β, add FIRST(β) − {ε} to FOLLOW(B).
If β is nullable, add FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B). This includes β = ε.
Repeat rules 2 and 3 until no set changes. One pass can add a set that enables another addition; this is the fixed point. A loop over all productions until stable is enough.

blocks.text: Example: E → T E′ adds FIRST(E′) − {ε} = {+} to FOLLOW(T). E′ is nullable, so FOLLOW(E) also goes to FOLLOW(T). F → ( E ) adds ) to FOLLOW(E).
FOLLOW never contains ε. Nullability changes what you add; ε itself is not a member.

figure.caption: All ten sets from the worked example, grouped where they come out equal. ε shows up only in FIRST of the nullable E′ and T′; every FOLLOW set carries $ and none carries ε.

spec.title: FIRST and FOLLOW for the expression grammar
spec.aria: A table lists the FIRST and FOLLOW sets of E, E′, T, T′ and F from the worked example, marking ε in the FIRST sets of E′ and T′ and $ in every FOLLOW set.

examples.question: For the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ), compute FIRST and FOLLOW for every nonterminal. The start symbol is E.
steps: Terminals: id, +, *, (, ), $. Nonterminals: E, E′, T, T′, F. Nullable: E′, T′.
FIRST(F) = {(, id}; FIRST(T) = {(, id}; FIRST(E) = {(, id}.
Start FOLLOW(E) = {$}. F → ( E ) adds ), so FOLLOW(E) = {), $}.
E → T E′ adds + to FOLLOW(T); E′ nullable adds FOLLOW(E) to FOLLOW(E′) and FOLLOW(T). So FOLLOW(E′) = {), $}; FOLLOW(T) = {+, ), $}.
T → F T′ adds * to FOLLOW(F); T′ nullable adds FOLLOW(T) to FOLLOW(T′), so FOLLOW(T′) = {+, ), $}.
T′ → * F T′ adds * to FOLLOW(F); T′ nullable adds FOLLOW(T′) to FOLLOW(F), so FOLLOW(F) = {*, +, ), $}.
examples.answer: FIRST(E) = FIRST(T) = FIRST(F) = {(, id}; FIRST(E′) = {+, ε}; FIRST(T′) = {*, ε}; FOLLOW(E) = FOLLOW(E′) = {), $}; FOLLOW(T) = FOLLOW(T′) = {+, ), $}; FOLLOW(F) = {*, +, ), $}.

traps: Putting ε in FIRST but not treating the nonterminal as nullable when computing FOLLOW; you then miss a whole FOLLOW set.
Writing ε in FOLLOW. FOLLOW holds terminals and $; absence is not a member.
Forgetting $ on the start symbol, so every FOLLOW set that depends on the start is wrong.
Stopping after one pass. FOLLOW can need several rounds before no set changes.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a nonterminal to be nullable?
quiz.a: A is nullable if A ⇒* ε, so it can derive the empty string.

quiz.q: Why is ε never placed in a FOLLOW set?
quiz.a: FOLLOW lists terminals that can follow a nonterminal. ε is the absence of a symbol, not a terminal.

quiz.q: For S → A B, A → a | ε, B → b, give FIRST(S) and FOLLOW(A). S is the start symbol.
quiz.a: FIRST(A) = {a, ε}; FIRST(B) = {b}; FIRST(S) = {a, b}. FOLLOW(S) = {$}. S → A B gives FIRST(B) = {b} to FOLLOW(A), so FOLLOW(A) = {b}.

quiz.q: In E → T E′, why does FOLLOW(T) get both + and )?
quiz.a: E′ follows T, so FIRST(E′) − {ε} = {+} goes to FOLLOW(T). E′ is nullable, so FOLLOW(E) = {), $} also goes to FOLLOW(T).

quiz.q: If FIRST(X) = {a, ε} and FIRST(Y) = {b}, what is FIRST(XY)?
quiz.a: Add FIRST(X) − {ε} = {a}; X is nullable, so add FIRST(Y) = {b}. The answer is {a, b}; ε is not added because Y is not nullable.

quiz.q: Why must the FOLLOW rules be repeated to a fixed point?
quiz.a: A set added late can enable another addition. Repeat until no FOLLOW set changes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as ANTLR and yacc compute FIRST and FOLLOW internally. LL(1) is a small corner of parsing; many modern languages use hand-written recursive descent or PEG parsers. FIRST and FOLLOW ideas reappear in grammar analysis tools and in error-message generation. Search for 'LL(1) FIRST FOLLOW' or 'nullable FIRST FOLLOW algorithm' to go further.
